newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire war sparks another refugee crisis.
newsitem.headline: Zaire war sparks another refugee crisis.

text.p: The sight of thousands of exhausted Hutu refugees trudging down jungle paths in eastern Zaire where armed rebels are pressing their advance has refocused world attention on the central African country's civil war.

Hundreds of bedraggled Hutus fleeing the fighting were spotted heading west towards the city of Kisangani on Monday, having already walked around 70 km (45 miles) from their camp at Tingi Tingi, seized by Tutsi-led rebels on Friday.
The rebels, apparently determined to build on a momentum of battlefield victories, pressed on from several fronts on Monday, declaring Kisangani as their next target.
A rebel statement broadcast on local radio in Goma gave Zaire's army generals a deadline of March 13 to lay down their arms. The rebels earlier rejected calls for a ceasefire.
Pope John Paul appealed for an end to the fighting, saying conditions in eastern Zaire were "an insult to human dignity".

"No man of goodwill can ignore the fate of these people who, in the regions touched by violence, live in conditions which are an insult to human dignity and where life is constantly endangered," he said in a speech to Zairean bishops who met him at the Vatican on Monday.
U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan told a news conference on Monday he believed an international military force could play a role in relieving the humanitarian crisis in Zaire.
"Unless we can get a ceasefire arranged...maybe we should study the possibility of using troops to create humanitarian corridors to evacuate the refugees," he said in The Hague.

Annan said he discussed "the tragic and compelling humanitarian situation" in Zaire with Dutch Foreign Aid Minister Jan Pronk. He would do so again on Tuesday with Prime Minister Wim Kok and Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo.
Reporters flown to eastern Zaire in a government army helicopter from Kisangani saw hundreds of refugees stretched out along the road about 150 km (100 miles) west of kisangani.
Some had only one shoe and many leaned on walking sticks with bandages wrapped around their weary legs.
Most of those who reached that far were aged under 30.
The Hutus said they fled the camp at Tingi Tingi, formerly home to some 170,000 refugees, on Friday after hearing mortar fire nearby. They had little idea where they would be going.
The governor of Upper Zaire Province said the Hutus would be diverted off the main road to Kisangani and received at the town of Ubundu 100 km (60 miles) south of the provincial capital.

"At Kisangani we already have too many problems with the displaced, with the local population, with unemployment, and with food shortages. We will direct the refugees towards Ubundu,' Governor Lombeya Basongo said.
Ubundu like Kisangani is situated on the banks of the vast Zaire river.
A Western businessman who has visited the town said it is surrounded by mangrove swamps with little opportunity for refugees to find food.
"It could be the largest cemetery in Zaire," he said.
Tutsi-led rebels who took up arms against the government of ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko in October have seized a long border strip and captured many important towns.
More than a million Hutus who fled violence in Burundi and Rwanda in 1993 and 1994 were initially trapped by the fighting. More than half that number returned to Rwanda late last year.

South Africa and the United States tried unsuccessfully last week to get rebel leader Laurent Kabila to agree a ceasefire. Kabila, who says his objective is to end Mobutu's 31-year rule, said he would only agree a truce if the president personally joined negotiations.
Mobutu is receiving cancer treatment in France.
